mcqs.question: A DAG has a valid topological order. What does that order actually guarantee?
options: That the order is the only valid topological order for that graph
That every node with no dependencies runs in parallel with every other such node
That for every directed edge u to v, u appears somewhere before v in the order — not necessarily immediately before
That the order matches the order nodes were originally added to the graph
mcqs.explanation: The only guarantee is relative ordering per edge — u somewhere before v, with no promise of adjacency. Most DAGs have many valid topological orders, so uniqueness isn't guaranteed, and the order alone doesn't directly encode a parallelization plan or preserve any original insertion order.

mcqs.question: In Kahn's algorithm, the final check is len(order) == n, returning None if it fails. What does a shorter-than-n output length signal?
options: The graph has more than one connected component
The graph has a cycle — some nodes never reached in-degree 0 because they were stuck in a mutual dependency
The in-degree array was initialized incorrectly
The graph is undirected rather than directed
mcqs.explanation: Nodes involved in a cycle can never have their in-degree fully reduced to 0 by processing only nodes outside the cycle, so they're never added to the queue or the output — leaving the final order shorter than the total node count. This isn't about component count, initialization bugs, or graph directionality; it's specifically the cycle signature.

mcqs.question: In DFS-based topological sort, why is a node pushed onto the finish stack AFTER exploring all of its neighbors, rather than when it's first visited?
options: Pushing on finish records that everything reachable from this node is already accounted for, which is what makes reversing the stack produce dependencies before dependents
Pushing on entry versus on finish produces identical results either way
It's purely a performance optimization with no effect on correctness
Pushing on entry would cause an infinite loop in cyclic graphs
mcqs.explanation: Finishing a node means everything reachable from it has already been fully explored and already pushed, so that node's dependencies are already lower on the stack — reversing then places dependencies first. Pushing on entry (discovery order) instead of finish would give a completely different, generally invalid ordering, and this is a correctness requirement, not a performance tweak or something related to loop termination.

mcqs.question: For a directed edge u to v in a DAG, what is guaranteed about their DFS finishing times?
options: u and v always finish at the exact same time
There's no guaranteed relationship between their finishing times
u always finishes before v
v always finishes before u, since v must be fully explored as part of exploring u's subtree before u itself can be marked finished
mcqs.explanation: Since v is reachable from u, DFS must completely finish exploring v (and everything below it) before it can mark u itself as finished — meaning v's finish time always precedes u's finish time for every edge u to v. That relationship is exactly what makes reversing the finish order produce a valid topological order; it's a proven relationship, not an unpredictable one.

mcqs.question: Which topological sort approach naturally exposes groups of nodes that could be processed in parallel at each stage?
options: DFS-based sort, via its reversed finish order
Kahn's algorithm, since each round of the queue represents nodes whose dependencies are all already satisfied
Neither approach exposes this information without extra bookkeeping
Both approaches expose this equally well by default
mcqs.explanation: Kahn's algorithm processes nodes in layers — everything with in-degree 0 initially, then everything that becomes in-degree 0 once that layer is removed — and each such layer is a genuine candidate for parallel execution, since none of them depend on each other. DFS-based sort produces only a single linear order with no natural notion of which nodes are independent of each other without additional analysis.

mcqs.question: A DFS-based topological sort is run on a graph without any cycle check, and the graph happens to contain a cycle. What's the likely outcome?
options: The function throws a clear, descriptive error explaining the cycle
The algorithm automatically switches to Kahn's algorithm as a fallback
It silently produces a garbage, invalid order with no indication anything is wrong
It correctly detects and reports the cycle without any additional code
mcqs.explanation: Plain DFS-based topological sort has no built-in cycle awareness — without an added gray/black check layered on top (the three-color method), it will complete and produce an ordering, just one that isn't actually valid, with nothing signaling the problem. It doesn't throw an error, doesn't fall back to another algorithm, and doesn't detect the cycle on its own the way Kahn's length check does.
